design_detail: Scoping review and evidence map (Joanna Briggs Institute and Cochrane scoping methods; reported to PRISMA-ScR), commissioned under Colorado House Bill 21-1317 to inform whether the THC concentration of cannabis products should be regulated. Seven databases searched in October 2021 and updated in July 2022; English language and human studies only; human studies of any epidemiological design that reported a THC concentration or a known high-concentration product. Artificial-intelligence-assisted title and abstract screening in DistillerSR; one reviewer extracted data, checked by senior reviewers; no risk-of-bias assessment, by design; no synthesis of results. The output is counts of studies by exposure, outcome and design, plus a public interactive evidence map (Tableau, not opened) of the 452 included studies. It is an inventory of what has been studied, not a summary of what was found.
can_establish: How much human research exists in which a THC concentration or a high-concentration product is reported: how many studies, of which designs, in which countries and with which outcomes; how they report exposure (concentration, frequency, duration, route); how many study concentrates (54 of 452) or THC concentration (189) directly and how many give data that could be pooled; how the strengths studied compare with market strengths the authors cite from other sources; and who funded the studies and how often interests were declared. It supports the statement that direct evidence on high-concentration products and health outcomes is limited and hard to combine.
cannot_establish: What any strength or product does to health: no study results are extracted, pooled or appraised, so nothing here says which outcomes concentrates raise or lower. Whether the 54 studies on concentrates, or the 189 on THC concentration, are good studies (no risk-of-bias assessment) or what they found. Dose or exposure: the authors state that THC concentration is not the same as dose. Completeness: searching was English-only and designed to be sensitive rather than specific, screening was AI-assisted with no recall figure, and one reviewer extracted each study, so studies may be missed or mis-coded. The market strengths quoted come from other sources (a 2018 seven-state survey and a Colorado market report), not from this review’s data. The Appendix (search strategy, study characteristics table), the evidence map and the protocol were not opened.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (a literature search). Seven databases, designed by a medical information specialist with controlled vocabulary and keywords and peer-reviewed against the PRESS checklist; initial search October 2021, update July 2022; English language and human studies only; no date limit; comments, editorials, interviews, news articles and letters excluded (Methods › Data Sources and Searches).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: human studies of any epidemiological design, in any country, age group, health status or outcome, on recreational or medicinal cannabis, that reported a THC concentration in any unit or described a product from which a high concentration could be inferred (for example a high-potency concentrate or dab). Excluded: animal, laboratory and simulation studies; studies reporting only a THC:CBD ratio; CBD-only or cannabinol-only products; dronabinol, nabilone and similar medicines (Methods › Study Selection Criteria).
sample.demographics: Included studies (452): 225 observational studies, 142 randomized trials, 51 case reports, 34 case series; earliest 1971, 60% (269) published 2017 to 2022; United States 220 (49%), United Kingdom 46 (10%), Canada 45 (10%) and 27 other countries; purpose of cannabis use medicinal 39%, recreational 15%, unintentional 4%, other 35%, not reported 19%; participants from newborns to adults over 65; 48 studies (11%) included any health-equity analysis and none analysed structural racism (Results › Characteristics of Included Studies).
sample.attrition: 49,729 unique records, 5,828 full-text reports, 452 included studies (Results, 1st paragraph; Figure 1, an image, not read). Reasons for excluding full-text reports were recorded (Methods › Study Selection › Full-text screening).
sample.selection_effects: English-only; searches sensitive rather than specific, and the authors say relevant studies may have been missed despite AI-assisted screening (Limitations). By design only studies that report a THC concentration or a known high-concentration product are included, so research on cannabis use in general lies outside the map. Most included studies concern generic cannabis types (284, 63%); products typically high in concentration (oils, concentrates, hash, extracts, skunk, resins) were examined in approximately 2% to 10% of all studies.

exposure.measurement: Whatever each primary study reported, extracted as written. THC concentration as a percentage in 172 studies (38%; 349 exposures) or in milligrams in 113 studies (25%; 143 exposures); route in 393 (87%); frequency of intake in 384 (85%); duration in 371 (82%). Units and indices vary (range, threshold, exact value, mean). The authors write that most studies did not capture all the elements of cannabis use needed to estimate exposure dose (Discussion › Exposure Assessment, 1st paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Route: inhalation 279 studies (62%), ingestion 174 (38%), sublingual 39 (9%), topical 31 (7%); a study can report more than one. THC as a percentage: median 12% (mean 17.4%, range 0% to 100%, interquartile range 3.6% to 24%). THC in milligrams: median 15 mg (mean 37.4, range 0.3 to 500, interquartile range 7.5 to 26). Median reported THC was below 50 mg or 25% for every outcome domain. Frequency most often daily (177 studies, 39%) (Results › Exposures; Results › Outcomes, 3rd paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Other substance use is not among the extracted data items listed in the Methods, and no analysis of it is reported (Methods › Data Collection).

comparison.controls: Not applicable at review level. Of the 452 studies, 212 (47%) had a control group; the review extracted details of the comparison exposure where there was one but does not compare outcomes between exposure groups.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable at review level; the confounding in the included studies was not assessed. The authors note that key populations, for example racial and ethnic minority groups, may be missing from the studies and that generalisability cannot be gauged without specific information on who uses which products (Discussion › Populations Studied).

outcomes.instruments: Outcomes were extracted as written in each study and sorted by the reviewers into 16 domains based on earlier reports on cannabis: mental health, neurologic, pain, cardiometabolic, gastrointestinal, psychosocial, sleep, substance use or dependence, respiratory, cancer, ocular, injury and death, immunity, sexual and reproductive health, pregnancy-related outcomes (mother), and pre-, peri- and neonatal outcomes (Methods › Study Selection Criteria › Health outcomes).
outcomes.validity_norms: No assessment of the validity of outcome measures in the included studies. The extraction form was piloted; one reviewer extracted each study and senior reviewers checked it.
outcomes.operationalization: Counts of studies by outcome domain (mental health 180, 40%; neurologic 134, 30%; pain 133, 29%; cardiometabolic 110, 24%; gastrointestinal 101, 22%; psychosocial 98, 22%; sleep 94, 21%) and by whether a study examined concentrates or THC concentration directly (54 and 189) or indirectly (62 and 114). The authors note that outcome domains are broad and that even a single outcome such as depression was measured in different ways (Results › Outcomes, 1st paragraph).

analysis.effect_sizes: None. The results are counts and percentages of studies. Of 452 studies, 54 (12%) examined a direct association between concentrates and a health outcome, 189 (42%) a direct association between THC concentration and an outcome, 114 (25%) an indirect association between THC concentration and outcomes and 62 (14%) an indirect association between concentrates and outcomes; 212 (47%) had a control group; outcomes were reported with effect estimates in 184 (41%), measures of precision in 274 (61%), significance tests in 335 (74%), sample size in 349 (77%) and raw data in 232 (51%) (Results › Potential for Evidence Synthesis).
analysis.preregistration_detail: A protocol was published on OSF Registries in 2021 (reference 16) and the Methods point to it for detail; the Methods say three authors were added because of their contributions after the protocol was published. The protocol itself was not opened, so deviations were not checked. A risk-of-bias assessment was not planned, as scoping methods allow (Methods › Data Collection, last paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: Not applicable in the usual sense, since there are no hypothesis tests. The Methods list five questions put to the evidence map; the full cross-tabulations sit in the map and Appendix Table A, which were not opened.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A large, varied literature (452 human studies, 1971 to 2022) in which only 54 studies (12%) examine concentrates and a health outcome directly and 189 (42%) examine THC concentration directly; most studies use generic cannabis; the median strength reported is 12% THC or 15 mg, below the market strengths the authors cite (Colorado flower averaging 19% and concentrates 68% in 2020); exposure is incompletely reported, outcomes and units are heterogeneous, and few studies give data that could be pooled. 6% of studies were funded by the cannabis industry and 13% had an author with a disclosed industry tie. The review reports no effects.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Conclusions say the review supports strong conclusions about the usefulness of the literature for characterising risks and benefits of the current marketplace, that major improvements in measuring and reporting exposure and outcomes are needed, that generalisability of the studies to today’s marketplace is seriously limited, and that high-quality evidence on whether THC concentration should be regulated is scarce. These are claims about the literature, and the counts support them. The Abstract’s wording about “strong conclusions” can be misread as a conclusion about health effects. The statement that high-quality evidence is scarce rests on counts of reporting features (for example, 47% with a control group), not on an appraisal of quality, which the review did not do. The Discussion’s reason for the low strengths studied (restriction of research cannabis to a federal supply) is stated as likely and is the authors’ inference from cited sources.

timeline.event: National Academies report on the health effects of cannabis, cited by the authors for the wide array of outcome domains studied (Discussion › Outcomes Studied).

Survey of THC strength in products sold in 7 US states (Cash et al., PLoS One; reference 22) and a Colorado regulated-market update (reference 23), the sources of the market strengths the authors compare with the strengths studied; not read.
Scoping-review protocol published on OSF Registries (reference 16); not opened.
This scoping review and evidence map; the authors say it is meant to be kept up to date as the literature grows (Discussion › Conclusions, 3rd paragraph).

replication.where_it_stands: A mapping exercise, not a finding to be replicated. No update of the map or full systematic review of its subsets was read. Controlled and naturalistic studies that measure intoxication or impairment after concentrates (Bidwell 2020, this batch) and the review of potency and mental ill health and addiction (Petrilli 2022, not yet readable) address parts of the gap the authors describe.

funding.funder: State of Colorado, as specified in House Bill 21-1317, which asked the Colorado School of Public Health for a systematic review of the physical and mental health effects of high-potency THC marijuana and concentrates; the funder was not involved in design, conduct or publication of the paper (Acknowledgments, 1st paragraph; Introduction, 2nd paragraph, which PMC shows under the Plain-Language Summary heading as its 3rd paragraph).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed (Conflicts of Interest section): L. Bero is a paid consultant as conflict-of-interest advisor for Health Canada, including its cannabis committees; G. S. Wang is a paid author for UpToDate for a chapter on cannabis intoxication; A. Brooks-Russell has research funding from the Institute of Cannabis Research (Colorado State University) and serves on the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment’s Marijuana Public Health Advisory Committee. No cannabis-industry or tobacco-industry funding or ties are declared. The review itself counted these in the studies it mapped: 25 (6%) were funded by the cannabis industry, 58 (13%) had an author with a disclosed industry tie, 24% reported no funding source and 32% no conflicts statement (Results › Characteristics of Included Studies, 4th paragraph).
funding.affiliations_note: The review was done at the Colorado School of Public Health at the state legislature’s request; the same state’s health department funded Monte 2019 and Bidwell 2020 (this batch), and one author sits on that department’s advisory committee. The authors state that none of the screeners had published eligible cannabis research (Methods › Quality control and quality assurance, 2nd paragraph). Recorded as a reason to read closely, not to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A full systematic review with risk-of-bias assessment and, where studies are comparable, meta-analysis of the subsets the map identifies (for example the 54 studies on concentrates), together with primary studies that measure exposure completely (product, THC content, frequency and route in standard units) and outcomes with shared instruments, in people using today’s products.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (human studies, any age or health status), exposure (a reported THC concentration or a known high-concentration product) and outcomes (any health outcome) are specified; no comparator is required (47% of included studies had a control group) and follow-up is not specified. A scoping review works from concept and context, not PICO.

A protocol was published on OSF Registries in 2021 (reference 16) and the Methods rely on it; three authors were added after its publication, which implies it came first. Question, search and criteria are in the protocol; a risk-of-bias assessment was not planned. Deviations are not discussed in the main text. The protocol was not opened.

The Introduction explains that the breadth of the policy question, the varied definitions of high concentration, the range of outcomes and the variety of designs suit a scoping review that maps rather than pools (Introduction, 3rd paragraph, which PMC shows under the Plain-Language Summary heading as its 4th paragraph).

Main text: seven databases; controlled vocabulary and keywords; designed by a medical information specialist and peer-reviewed with the PRESS checklist; no date limit; October 2021, updated July 2022; English and human studies only, with no justification of the language limit in the main text; no reference-list, registry or grey-literature search described. The full strategy and any justification are in the Appendix, which was not opened.

Full-text eligibility was judged independently by two screeners, with disagreements settled by a senior reviewer. Title and abstract screening was AI-assisted: the algorithm was trained on 1,000 records coded independently by two senior screeners, then ranked the rest; 2% of all decisions were re-checked and an error-check tool compared human decisions with AI rankings. No agreement figure or recall estimate is given for the title and abstract stage.
One reviewer extracted each study into a piloted form and senior reviewers checked it (the Abstract says a subset was verified).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Reasons for excluding full-text reports were recorded (Methods › Full-text screening) and may appear in the flow diagram (an image) or the Appendix; no list of excluded studies is cited in the main text. The Appendix and the OSF project were not opened.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Designs, countries, purposes of use, populations, exposures and outcomes are described in aggregate; the study-by-study description is in the evidence map and Appendix Table A, neither opened.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: None was made, by design, because of the heterogeneity of designs; the authors say it could follow if the studies are taken forward to a full systematic review (Limitations).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Extracted for every study and summarised: 24% reported no funding source, 6% were cannabis-industry funded, 13% had an author with a disclosed industry tie.
No synthesis of results was attempted; the review counts studies.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: No risk of bias was assessed, so none is carried into the interpretation. The statement that high-quality evidence is scarce rests on counts of reporting features, not on a quality appraisal.

No results were pooled, so there is no heterogeneity of results to explain; the Discussion explains how the diversity of exposures, outcomes and units prevents synthesis and proposes standardised reporting.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding by the State of Colorado, the role of the funder and the authors’ interests are reported as printed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: items 4 and 7 can be judged only from the Appendix and the OSF project, which were not opened, so both are recorded as no information. AMSTAR 2 is built for reviews that pool the effects of an intervention. Applied as written to this scoping review and evidence map, two critical items are “no” (no risk-of-bias assessment of the included studies, which scoping methods omit by design, and so no account of risk of bias in the interpretation), which gives critically low confidence whatever items 4 and 7 turn out to be. That rating is a mechanical result of what the review set out to do, not a finding that the mapping is careless: a protocol was published, seven databases were searched with a peer-reviewed strategy, full-text selection was in duplicate, the funding of included studies was extracted and counted, and the conclusions stay within what a map can show. The review may be cited for what has been studied and how it was reported (counts of studies, exposures, outcomes, funding) and for the gaps it identifies; it should not be cited for any effect of high-concentration products.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC10632847 (abstract, plain-language summary, Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion, Conclusions, acknowledgments, conflicts of interest, reference list and the author-information panel read as text; Figures 1 to 3 are images, their legends were read and the PRISMA numbers were taken from the text; the Appendix (search strategy, Appendix Table A), the interactive evidence map and the OSF protocol were not opened)

key_findings.finding: Searches identified 49,729 unique records, 5,828 full-text reports and 452 included studies: 225 observational studies, 142 randomized trials, 51 case reports and 34 case series. The earliest was published in 1971 and 60% (269) in 2017 to 2022.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st (unlabelled) paragraph; Results › Characteristics of Included Studies, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Few studies give data that could support synthesis: 54 (12%) examined a direct association between concentrates and a health outcome and 189 (42%) a direct association between THC concentration and an outcome; 114 (25%) and 62 (14%) examined indirect associations; 212 (47%) had a control group; effect estimates were reported in 184 (41%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Potential for Evidence Synthesis, paragraph
key_findings.note: Counts of study features; they say nothing about what the studies found.

key_findings.finding: Strengths studied: when THC was given as a percentage (172 studies, 349 exposures) the median was 12% (mean 17.4%, range 0% to 100%, interquartile range 3.6% to 24%); when given in milligrams (113 studies, 143 exposures) the median was 15 mg (mean 37.4, range 0.3 to 500, interquartile range 7.5 to 26). Median reported THC was below 50 mg or 25% for every outcome domain. Units and indices varied.
key_findings.locator: Results › Exposures, 3rd paragraph; Results › Outcomes, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: The authors state that THC concentration is not the same as dose (Methods › Study Selection Criteria › THC concentration of products, 2nd paragraph).

key_findings.finding: Most studies concerned generic cannabis types (284, 63%); products typically high in concentration (oils, concentrates, hash, extracts, skunk, resins) were examined in approximately 2% to 10% of all studies. Route was reported in 393 studies (87%): inhalation 62%, ingestion 38%, sublingual 9%, topical 7%. Frequency was reported in 384 (85%), most often daily (177, 39%); duration in 371 (82%).

Outcome domains: mental health 180 studies (40%), neurologic 134 (30%), pain 133 (29%), cardiometabolic 110 (24%), gastrointestinal 101 (22%), psychosocial 98 (22%), sleep 94 (21%). A single outcome such as depression was measured in different ways in different studies.

Funding and interests in the included studies: 24% (109) did not report a funding source and 32% (143) did not report whether authors had conflicts of interest; 25 studies (6%) were funded by the cannabis industry and 58 (13%) had an author who disclosed a financial tie with the industry.
key_findings.locator: Results › Characteristics of Included Studies, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Only 48 studies (11%) included any analysis of a health-equity measure, 41 (9%) analysed or stratified by health-equity subgroups, 6 (1%) focused exclusively on historically excluded populations, and none analysed structural racism or inequalities.
key_findings.locator: Results › Characteristics of Included Studies, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Market strengths the authors cite from other sources: a 2018 survey of products sold in 7 US states found most products between 15% and 30% THC; in Colorado the average THC of flower assayed rose from 14% to 19% between 2014 and 2020 and that of concentrates from 46% to 68%. They describe the median of 12% studied as well below what is currently on the market and attribute the low strengths studied, as likely, to the restriction of research cannabis in the United States to a federal supply that lacks concentrates.
key_findings.note: Market figures are quoted from a published survey and a Colorado market report, not measured in this review; the reason for the low strengths is the authors’ inference.

key_findings.finding: The authors write that most studies failed to capture all the elements of cannabis use needed to estimate exposure dose, and recommend that studies at least report THC concentration, product used, frequency of use and route, in THC units that can be standardised.

Conclusions: the review supports strong conclusions about the usefulness of the literature for characterising risks and benefits of the current marketplace; there are serious limitations in the generalisability of the studies to the current marketplace or to the people who buy its products; high-quality evidence on whether THC concentration should be regulated is scarce.
key_findings.note: “Strong” refers to conclusions about the literature, not about health effects.

key_findings.finding: Stated limits: searches were sensitive rather than specific; relevant studies may have been missed despite AI-assisted screening; heterogeneity of designs did not allow risk-of-bias assessment of individual studies; incomplete and inconsistent reporting left gaps in the extracted data.

reporting_issues.issue: The Abstract and Conclusions say the review supports strong conclusions concerning the utility of the literature. Read alone, “strong conclusions” can be taken as a conclusion about health effects; the review extracts and reports no effects.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite as an inventory of studies and a statement about gaps; do not cite as evidence of any effect.

reporting_issues.issue: The Abstract says one person extracted data and a senior reviewer verified a subset; the Methods say the single extractor’s work was checked by senior reviewers without saying how much.
reporting_issues.consequence: How much of the extraction was independently checked is unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: AI-assisted title and abstract screening: the Methods describe training on 1,000 records and continuous re-ranking of the rest but give no recall estimate, stopping rule or count of records screened by people at that stage.
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of any shortfall in studies found is unknown; the authors say relevant studies may have been missed.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods name the authors added after the protocol as R. L., J.-P. O. and T. W. K.; the author list and the screening paragraph give T. W. Y.

Counts for products typically high in concentration are given as a single range (approximately 2% to 10% of all studies) in the text; the breakdown by product type is in Figure 2 and Appendix Table A, neither read.
reporting_issues.consequence: How many studies examined each kind of concentrate cannot be read from the text.
